readings.title: Song of the Ducks
readings.challenge: Count ducks in a picture you can only hear, then find the surprise duck.
readings.focus: A counting game about ducks turns out to be about the child on the speaker’s lap.
readings.context: Mary Mapes Dodge wrote this poem to go with a picture of ducks; we have only the words, so the child can imagine or draw the ducks. Trim means neat; to linger is to stay a while. Point with a finger as you read, as the poem asks.

excerpt.locator: “Song of the Ducks,” the complete poem; opens “ONE little black duck, one little gray, Six little white ducks, running out to play; One…”; closes “…One lazy black duck, taking quite a nap; One little precious duck, here on mamma's lap!”.

questions.prompt: How many baby ducks is the white lady-duck taking for a swim?
facilitatorNotes: Eight little baby ducks.
evidence: Eight little baby ducks, bound for a swim!

questions.prompt: Find two ducks that are doing something different from the rest.
facilitatorNotes: One holds up its wings, one makes water-rings, one runs from the water, one swims off alone, one stands on a stone. Children can act one out.
evidence: One little bobbing duck, making water-rings,
One very brave duck, swimming off alone,

questions.prompt: Who is the “other duck,” the nicest duck of all? How do you know?
facilitatorNotes: The child being read to: this duck has no feathers and a sweet small mouth, jumps on the speaker’s knee, cannot swim, and ends up on mamma’s lap. Let the child enjoy finding out it is them.
evidence: He hasn't any feathers, and his mouth is sweet and small;
One little precious duck, here on mamma's lap!

readings.title: That’s What We’d Do
readings.challenge: Imagine being an owl and follow the plan step by step.
readings.focus: Two friends picture what they would do together if they were owls in the moonlight.
readings.context: This poem plays “let’s pretend.” A bough is a branch; “beyond a doubt” means certainly. Owls come out when the moon is up. Read it to the child as “you,” with yourself as “I,” and wink when the poem winks.

excerpt.locator: “That's What We'd Do,” the complete poem; opens “IF you were an owl, And I were an owl, And this were a tree, And the moon came out, I…”; closes “…Why, you'd sing to me, And I'd sing to you; That's what we'd do, When the moon came out.”.

questions.prompt: What has to happen before the two owls do anything?
facilitatorNotes: They must be owls in a tree, and the moon must come out.
evidence: And this were a tree,
And the moon came out,

questions.prompt: What would the two owls do on the bough?
facilitatorNotes: Stand there together and wink at each other, and later sing to each other. Children can wink back.
evidence: You'd wink at me,
And I'd wink at you;

questions.prompt: Why do you think the speaker wants to be an owl together with “you”?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker wants to be close and share everything: standing together, a rose, winking and singing. It shows friendship or love. A child who says the speaker just likes owls can be asked why it is “we two.”
evidence: We would stand, we two,
I'd give you a rose

readings.title: Two Little Froggies
readings.challenge: Hear two small stories and find how they meet.
readings.focus: Hungry frogs wait on the bank while cheerful ants march off to the bogs, and the last line joins the two.
readings.context: Mary Mapes Dodge wrote these jingles for children. Liquor here just means liquid, the puddle water; meat means food. Bogs are wet, muddy places; gayly means happily; a dainty dinner is a tasty one.
readings.contentNote: The frogs eat the forty little ants.

excerpt.locator: “Two Little Froggies,” the complete poem; opens “TWO little froggies they sighed to one another: "Our puddle is all liquor and no meat.”; closes “…little ants never dreamed they were going Just to make a dainty dinner for the frogs.”.

questions.prompt: Why are the two little froggies unhappy with their puddle?
facilitatorNotes: It is all water and no food. They hope to find something good to eat on the bank.
evidence: Our puddle is all liquor and no meat.

questions.prompt: Where do the forty little ants say they are going, and how do they feel?
facilitatorNotes: To the bogs, and they say it happily. Ask what the ants might expect to find there.
evidence: Forty little ants said gayly to their mother:
"O mother! we are going to the bogs;"

questions.prompt: What do the ants not know? Why is the ending a surprise?
facilitatorNotes: That they are walking right to the hungry frogs, who will eat them for dinner. Some children will feel sorry for the ants and some will laugh; the jingle allows both.
evidence: And maybe we'll see something good to eat.
Just to make a dainty dinner for the frogs.

readings.title: Pussy’s Class
readings.challenge: Follow a lesson in which the pupils will not learn one of the things they are taught.
readings.focus: A mother cat teaches her kittens to meow, purr and scratch; they will not hiss or scratch, and she lets them go, fondly.
readings.context: Mary Mapes Dodge wrote these rhymes for children in America. Here a mother cat holds a class for her kittens. A perfume rare is a special sweet smell; a sharper tone is a crosser voice; “pshaw” is a sound of impatience; “Stpisss!” is a cat’s hiss; fond means loving. Let the child meow, purr and try the hiss for the kittens.
readings.contentNote: The mother cat teaches her kittens to scratch children who tease them, boxes their ears with her softest paw, and calls them “sweet little idiots.”

excerpt.locator: “Pussy's Class,” the complete poem; opens “"NOW children," said Puss, as she shook her head, "It is time your morning lesson was…”; closes “…Ah well, I was once the same, I suppose"-- And she looked very wise and rubbed her nose.”.

questions.prompt: What do the kittens say when they want a drink, and what do they do when children are good?
facilitatorNotes: They meow loudly for a drink, and purr softly for good children. Let the child do both.
evidence: You ought to have heard how those kittens meow'd!
And the kittens purred as soft as they could.

questions.prompt: What does the mother cat say the kittens must do when children are rough? What do the kittens think about that?
facilitatorNotes: Use their claws. The kittens feel sure they will never need such weapons, and they will not even hiss.
evidence: You must use your claws when children are rough!
They felt quite sure they never should need

questions.prompt: At the end she sends them off to play. Is the mother cat cross with her kittens, or loving?
facilitatorNotes: Mostly loving: she is called their “fond mamma,” calls them sweet, and remembers she was the same once. Some children will point out that she boxed their ears and called them idiots, so she is a little cross too; both readings use the poem.
evidence: said the fond mamma;
Ah well, I was once the same, I suppose

readings.title: The Sand Man
readings.challenge: Listen for all the places where sleep catches children.
readings.focus: A make-believe traveller with sleepy sand visits every child, though no one ever sees him come or go.
readings.context: The Sand Man is a make-believe figure from old stories who sprinkles sand in children’s eyes to make them sleepy. Elfish means like an elf; a rover is a wanderer; tricksome means playful; drowsy means sleepy; lambkins are little lambs; fragrant means sweet-smelling; whence and whither mean from where and to where. Read it more and more softly.

excerpt.locator: “The Sand Man,” the complete poem; opens “OHO! but he travels the country over, The queer little, kind little, elfish rover!…”; closes “…knows; For just when the right time comes to peep, All the children are falling asleep.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Sand Man carry, and what does he do with it?
facilitatorNotes: A silvery horn full of sleepy sand, which he shakes over flowers, lambs and birds and sprinkles over children’s heads.
evidence: A silvery horn full of sleepy sand,
And sprinkles his sand over children's heads,

questions.prompt: Where do the children fall asleep?
facilitatorNotes: On the carpet, on chairs, curled up on the stairs, in the grass, deep in the hay, and in their mother’s arms. Children may say where they once fell asleep.
evidence: Some curled up on the nursery stairs;
Some hidden deep in the fragrant hay,

questions.prompt: Does anyone know where the Sand Man comes from? What do you think really makes us sleepy?
facilitatorNotes: Nobody knows, because he is make-believe. Children may say playing hard, the dark, or a warm bed; the poem gives sleep a friendly face instead of a reason.
evidence: Every one wonders and nobody knows;
All the children are falling asleep.

readings.title: What They Say
readings.challenge: Hear the sound each toy makes and what it seems to say.
readings.focus: A boy’s toys each speak in their own noise, and all together cheer for racket.
readings.context: Mary Mapes Dodge wrote these rhymes for children in America. A boy is playing with his toys: a drum, a trumpet, a whip, a pop-gun (a toy that shoots out a cork or stick with a pop) and a toy sword. Bub is a pet name for a little boy; racket means noise; the lash is the long string of a whip; a manikin is a little man. Give each toy its own voice.
readings.contentNote: The toy pop-gun and toy sword talk about firing and cutting (“cut 'em in bits!”); the gun also warns, “See that you fire in nobody's eye.”

excerpt.locator: “What They Say,” the complete poem; opens “WHAT does the drum say? "Rub-a-dub-dub! Rub-a-dub, rub-a-dub! Pound away, bub! Make as…”; closes “…for fun! Babies no longer, but stout little men, Racket forever! and racket again!"”.

questions.prompt: What sound does the drum make, and what sound does the trumpet make?
facilitatorNotes: The drum goes “Rub-a-dub-dub!” and the trumpet “Toot-a-toot-too!” Children can drum and toot.
evidence: Rub-a-dub-dub!
Toot-a-toot-too!

questions.prompt: Which toy gives the boy a safety rule? What is the rule?
facilitatorNotes: The pop-gun: never fire it into anyone’s eye.
evidence: See that you fire in nobody's eye.

questions.prompt: What do all the toys say together at the end? Who do you think is really saying it?
facilitatorNotes: “Hurrah for fun!” and “Racket forever!” Many children will say it is really the boy, proud to be no longer a baby, and the toys speak his feelings. Some may enjoy imagining the toys really talking; the poem allows both.
evidence: Hurrah for fun!
Babies no longer, but stout little men,

readings.title: The Frost-King
readings.challenge: Decide whether a stern-looking character is kind or unkind.
readings.focus: Winter frost is pictured as a pale king who freezes the land but also makes snow, ice and fun.
readings.context: The Frost-King is winter’s frost pictured as a king. Hoary means white with frost; chill means cold; birdlings are little birds; wrath means anger. Coasting means sledding downhill. Jack is Jack Frost, who in stories paints ice patterns on windows. “Till Earth grows young again” means until spring.

excerpt.locator: “The Frost-King,” the complete poem; opens “OHO! have you seen the Frost-King, A-marching up the hill? His hoary face is stern and…”; closes “…Till gone are hill and plain: Whenever Winter comes to stay, The hoary King shall reign.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Frost-King look like, and what does his touch do?
facilitatorNotes: His face is white, stern and pale, and his touch is icy cold. He sends the birds south and makes the brooks still by freezing them.
evidence: His hoary face is stern and pale,
He bids the brooks be still;

questions.prompt: What fun does the Frost-King make for children?
facilitatorNotes: Snow for sledding, frozen rivers for skating, and Jack Frost’s merry tricks that call the children out to play.
evidence: That coasting boys may play.
That skating crowds may shout;

questions.prompt: The poem says he marches “not in wrath or cruelty.” Is the Frost-King kind or unkind?
facilitatorNotes: He looks stern and makes everything cold, but he is not angry: he rests to watch the sunbeams and makes snow and ice for play. Children may say he is both, which fits a king who is strict but fair.
evidence: Yet not in wrath or cruelty
He will often rest at noontime,

readings.title: After the Winter
readings.challenge: Hear everything that is coming with summer, one cheer at a time.
readings.focus: A list of birds, insects, flowers and fruit, each greeted with “hurrah!”, builds up to the joy of being alive.
readings.context: Mary Mapes Dodge wrote these rhymes for children in America. Katydids are big green insects, like grasshoppers, that sing at night; fire-flies are beetles that glow in the dark; laden means loaded; mites are tiny creatures; these corn-fields are fields of tall maize. Let the child shout every “hurrah!”

excerpt.locator: “After the Winter,” the complete poem; opens “THE summer is coming--hurrah! Old winter has gone for good. The summer is coming--hurrah!…”; closes “…good and glad: It's the grandest world--hurrah! hurrah! That ever we children have had.”.

questions.prompt: Name some of the creatures that are coming. Which one would you most like to see?
facilitatorNotes: Chickens, turkeys and ducks, tadpoles, crickets, katydids, fireflies, bumble-bees and swallows. Any choice with a reason counts.
evidence: The chickens are coming--hurrah!
The swallows are coming--hurrah!

questions.prompt: What will the children do with the daisies, the fruit and the corn-fields?
facilitatorNotes: Weave the daisies into chains, feast on the fruit, and hide in the tall corn.
evidence: We'll weave them in many a chain:
We'll hide in them by-and-by.

questions.prompt: The poem ends by calling this “the grandest world.” How do all the hurrahs lead up to that?
facilitatorNotes: Each new thing that is coming adds more happiness, until the children shout that it is jolly just to be alive. Children may name the one thing that would make summer grand for them.
evidence: Oh! it's jolly to be alive!
It's the grandest world--hurrah! hurrah!

readings.title: Out of the Shell
readings.challenge: Hear a newly hatched duckling speak for itself.
readings.focus: A brand-new duckling complains about its egg as if it had been a poor, cramped little house.
readings.context: The duckling has just hatched from its egg. “A duck of a bird” is a joke, because “duck” was also a word for a darling. Mean here means poor and shabby; a cramp is a tight squeeze; “thought me a spoon” means thought me silly. Read in a small, cross, proud voice.

excerpt.locator: “Out of the Shell,” the complete poem; opens “WELL, I'm out, after all! And I'll say, on my word, That's a pretty mean house For a duck…”; closes “…and dad May have thought me a spoon, But they'll not get me back In that thing very soon.”.

questions.prompt: What does the duckling call its eggshell?
facilitatorNotes: A pretty mean house: too small and poor for such a fine bird.
evidence: That's a pretty mean house

questions.prompt: What was it like inside the shell?
facilitatorNotes: The duckling could not stand up or sit down and lay squeezed from toes to head. Children can curl up small to show it.
evidence: Why, I couldn't stand up,
But I lay in a cramp

questions.prompt: Will the duckling ever go back into its shell? Why is that funny?
facilitatorNotes: “Not very soon,” it says, as if it might choose to; of course it never can. The joke is that it talks as if it had a choice.
evidence: But they'll not get me back
In that thing very soon.
